text:
Mammalian cells must maintain an intracellular reducing environment for survival (1). Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are generated as normal cellular metabolic byproducts (2), but an increase in ROS levels can induce oxidative stress that can lead to an inflammatory response (2). The thioredoxin system (thioredoxin/thioredoxin reductase/NADPH) is a crucial ubiquitous mechanism that protects against oxidative stress by its disulfide reductase function (3, 4, 5). The thioredoxin system is essential for mammals, as mice without thioredoxin-1 die shortly after implantation (6).

Thioredoxin-Interacting Protein (TXNIP) is a member of the arrestin domain–containing protein family (4, 7, 8). Members of this protein family, including TXNIP, play important roles in gluconeogenesis (9, 10, 11), adipogenesis (12), and fructose metabolism (13, 14). The absence of TXNIP can cause hyperlipidemia (15), hypoglycemia (11), decreased hepatic glucose production (HGP) (11), obesity (16), and increased beta cell survival (17). The TXNIP protein also participates in the regulation of peripheral glucose metabolism in humans (18). TXNIP is distinct from the other arrestin domain–containing proteins in its ability to bind to thioredoxin (4). TXNIP binds covalently to reduced thioredoxin and thus can inhibit thioredoxin disulfide reductase activity in vitro (19). TXNIP does not interact with oxidized thioredoxin or catalytic mutants of thioredoxin (4). The biochemistry of the TXNIP–thioredoxin bond is well characterized (4, 19, 20, 21). The key cysteine C247 of TXNIP is required for interaction with thioredoxin, as revealed by biochemistry and crystallography experiments (19, 20).

Transmembrane 7 Superfamily Member 2 (TM7SF2) is a transmembrane protein that resides in the endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear membranes and has C14-sterol reductase activity to assist the conversion of lanosterol to cholesterol in mammalian cells (22). In addition to its role in cholesterol biosynthesis, the Tm7sf2 gene can regulate insulin signaling (23, 24) and inflammation (25). In mice, Tm7sf2 was recently identified to be a tissue-specific nuclear envelope transmembrane protein that directs liver-specific patterns of radial genome organization for gene positioning (24). In addition to being a liver gene expression regulator, human TM7SF2 has also been shown to interact with an intracellular redox sensor protein in vitro (26).

The mechanism of diet-related insulin resistance is incompletely resolved. Improving diet-induced hepatic insulin resistance is a primary target for the cure of type 2 diabetes. Akt phosphorylation and consequent suppression of gluconeogenesis are central to the liver insulin response, but how hepatocyte signaling networks are dysregulated during a high-fat diet (HFD) and oxidative stress remains unclear. Increased oxidative stress has been extensively studied in metabolic diseases, including insulin resistance (27). Since TXNIP is molecularly positioned to sense redox potential and regulate metabolism, we explored the role of the unique redox-sensitive cysteine of TXNIP in mammalian metabolism. Our results show that mice with genetic editing of this single cysteine in TXNIP have altered lipid species profiles, increased hepatic insulin sensitivity and signaling, and decreased liver inflammation in the setting of an HFD. We also show that expression of Tm7sf2 is elevated in HFD-fed TXNIP C247S livers, and Tm7sf2 can regulate the insulin signaling pathway in liver cells under ROS-stress conditions, providing insight into the underlying mechanism of insulin resistance in hepatocytes during oxidative stress. We provide data that a cholesterol biosynthesis transmembrane protein plays an unexpected role in providing a missing link between oxidative state and hepatic insulin signaling. Together, our findings define a fundamental intersection between redox biology and mammalian hepatic metabolism.

We first sought insight into the role of the TXNIP–thioredoxin interaction in different organisms. Gathering data through available protein databases for TXNIP, we observed that the “..HIISGTCASW..” amino acid sequence that is known to bind human thioredoxin based on human TXNIP–thioredoxin coexpression studies (20) and includes the key C247 residue is only present in mammals (Fig. 1A). Most fish also bear a cysteine residue at approximately position 250 in a similar “..HIISGMCDMW..” amino acid sequence; it is currently unknown whether the piscine TXNIP binds thioredoxin. To evaluate the role of the TXNIP–thioredoxin interaction on in vivo metabolism, we generated a TXNIP C247S (or C247S) mouse model using the CRISPR–Cas9 technique. For the conversion of the cysteine 247 residue to serine, we mutated the TGC sequence to ATG in exon 5 (Fig. 1B). Cysteine and serine differ only in the exchange of a sulfur atom with oxygen; therefore, the amino acid position retains similar size while losing its redox sensitivity (28). The mutation was confirmed by both a new SpeI restriction site generated by the ATG mutation and Sanger sequencing (Fig. S1, A and B). We backcrossed the knock-in alleles for five generations to breed out potential off-target modifications and confirmed Mendelian ratios of allele inheritance. We also performed targeted locus amplification (TLA) sequencing to ensure the accurate integration of the mutated sequences into the native TXNIP loci, with no evidence of incorrect or off-target integration events (Fig. S1C). The pups appeared healthy, with a normal phenotype. We followed the body weights of the mice from 6 to 12 weeks of age and found no difference between groups by 12 weeks of age (Fig. S1D).

We performed insulin tolerance tests (ITTs), glucose tolerance tests (GTTs), and pyruvate tolerance tests (PTTs) on 12-week-old chow-fed WT, TXNIP C247S, and TXNIP KO mice. TXNIP KO mice were more insulin sensitive compared with WT mice as previously described (16), but we did not observe more insulin sensitivity in TXNIP C247S mice compared with WT mice (Fig. 1, C–E). We collected plasma samples from chow-fed WT, TXNIP C247S, and TXNIP KO mice after a 4-h fast to assess plasma lipid profiles. A hexosylceramide (d18:1/20:0) was measured to be lower in plasma of the TXNIP C247S group compared with the WT and TXNIP KO groups (Fig. 2A). Lysophosphatidylcholines (LPCs) are essential plasma lipids that control oxidative stress, NLR family pyrin domain–containing 3 (NLRP3)-mediated inflammation, and inflammatory markers such as tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) (29). Low levels of plasma LPCs are positively correlated with type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and aging (30, 31, 32, 33). We observed that plasma levels of several LPC species were elevated in C247S mice compared with both WT and TXNIP KO groups (Fig. 2, B–F). We observed the following changes in C247S mice plasma LPC levels compared with WT mice: 23% increase for LPC 14:0, 37% increase for LPC 16:1, 23% increase for LPC 20:2, 45% increase for LPC 20:5, and 36% increase for LPC 22:5 species. Since there were alterations in the lipid metabolism of TXNIP C247S mice, we placed these mice on a 60% HFD for 8 weeks to study their metabolic phenotypes under high fat–induced ROS-stress conditions. Following an HFD, TXNIP C247S mice had improved insulin tolerance compared with WT mice but did not have improved glucose or pyruvate tolerance (Fig. 2, G–I). As in controls, TXNIP KO mice also had elevated insulin sensitivity compared with WT mice as expected (16) (Fig. 2G).

To delineate the organs responsible for improved insulin sensitivity, we performed a standardized hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic clamp experiment with [3-3H]glucose infusion to assess whole-body glucose turnover and HGP and a bolus injection of [1–14C]2-deoxyglucose to measure insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in individual metabolic organs in 8-week HFD-fed mice. We and others have previously shown that TXNIP KO mice are more insulin sensitive compared with WT mice after an HFD (16, 34, 35). Both TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO mice showed increased insulin sensitivity compared with the WT mice, and TXNIP KO mice were more insulin sensitive than TXNIP C247S mice based on the glucose infusion rates during insulin clamps (Fig. 3A). Whole-body glucose turnover rates were significantly elevated in both TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO groups compared with WT controls (Fig. 3B). Hepatic insulin action, measured as insulin-mediated suppression of HGP, was increased significantly in the TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO mice compared with WT controls after an HFD (Fig. 3C). This was due to a lower HGP during the insulin clamp, whereas basal HGP was not altered in these groups (15.9 mg/kg/m for WT, 20 mg/kg/m for TXNIP C247S, and 21.5 mg/kg/m for TXNIP KO groups), indicating the improved ability of insulin to inhibit gluconeogenesis in the livers of TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO mice (Fig. 3D). These data pointed to the protection of TXNIP C247S mice from HFD-induced hepatic and whole-body insulin resistance because of the single amino acid mutation in TXNIP protein compared with WT mice. Five-hour fasted insulin levels tended to be higher in HFD-fed WT mice than in TXNIP C247S (p = 0.06) and TXNIP KO mice. The lower insulin levels in TXNIP KO mice were consistent with improved insulin sensitivity in these mice (Fig. 3E). In contrast, insulin-stimulated glucose uptake rates in white adipose tissue (epididymal) were similar in TXNIP C247S mice compared with WT mice (Fig. 3F). Also, only the TXNIP KO group had elevated skeletal muscle glucose uptake rates compared with WT mice (Fig. 3G). These results suggest that increased insulin sensitivity in the TXNIP C247S group was primarily because of protection from diet-induced hepatic insulin resistance. Despite significant changes in insulin resistance in TXNIP C247S mice, we did not observe any differences in TXNIP protein levels (Fig. S1E). We also did not detect a difference in oxidative stress marker GSH and GSH/GSSG ratios between WT and TXNIP C247S mice livers under chow diet where insulin sensitivities are similar between WT and TXNIP C247S groups (Fig. 3H). However, we noted lower GSH and GSH/GSSG values in HFD-fed TXNIP C247S livers compared with HFD-fed WT mice livers along with improved insulin sensitivity (Fig. 3I). There was no difference between groups for thioredoxin activity (Fig. S2A) between the TXNIP C247S group and WT group livers. There was no correlation between body weight and hepatic insulin action levels of the mice included in the hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic clamp studies (Fig. S2B). To confirm increased insulin signaling in the livers of TXNIP C247S mice, we performed Western blot analyses on insulin-stimulated tissues and detected increased Akt phosphorylation in the livers of the TXNIP C247S group compared with WT controls (Fig. 3J). These data suggest improved insulin signaling in the livers of HFD-fed TXNIP C247S mice. We did not observe a change in AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) or mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) phosphorylation in HFD-fed TXNIP C247S livers compared with HFD-fed WT livers (Fig. S2, C and D).

We measured liver free fatty acid levels in chow- and HFD-fed mice. We did not detect a difference between hepatic free fatty acid levels in the groups on a chow diet (Fig. S3A); however, the TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO groups tended to have decreased hepatic free fatty acid levels compared with WT controls on an HFD (Fig. S3B). We did not detect a difference in the liver triglyceride levels between groups (Fig. S3C). Plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate levels were elevated in TXNIP KO mice compared with WT and TXNIP C247S groups under chow diet and HFD (Fig. S3D). Liver hexosylceramide (d18:1, 20:0) and LPC levels of the WT and TXNIP C247S mice were similar following an HFD (Fig. S3, E–J).

We then performed bulk RNA-Seq analysis to identify the altered genes and pathways in the TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO livers under HFD conditions. The gene expression differences in the livers of TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO mice compared with WT mice were surprisingly restricted given the metabolic phenotypes (Fig. 4, A–D). As Kyoto Encylopedia of Genes and Genomes database pathway analysis suggested, out of several genes that showed altered gene expression, the majority belonged to the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway (Fig. 5A). Genes that code for enzymes in the cholesterol synthesis pathway (Idi1, Fdps, Sqle, Cyp51, Tm7sf2, Nsdhl, Hsd7b17, and Dhcr7) were upregulated in the TXNIP C247S mouse livers compared with WT controls (Fig. 5B, the upregulated genes are highlighted in yellow boxes). We also validated the increased expressions of these cholesterol genes according to the RNA-Seq data in the TXNIP C247S group in a different cohort of mouse livers by quantitative PCR (Fig. 5C). The plasma total and free cholesterol levels were increased in mice by HFD (Fig. S3, L and M). One of the upregulated genes in TXNIP C247S mouse livers involved in cholesterol synthesis was particularly of interest. The Tm7sf2 gene codes for a protein that enables delta14-sterol reductase activity (22) and plays roles in several essential pathways. The TM7SF2 protein is a paralog of the Lamin-B receptor (LBR), which is also responsible for sterol reduction (24). This protein resides on nuclear and endoplasmic reticulum membranes (24). In the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway, the delta14-sterol reductase enzyme that the Tm7sf2 gene encodes can reduce C14-unsaturated sterols (36). The Tm7sf2 protein improves insulin sensitivity in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (23) and increases Akt phosphorylation in mouse livers (24), linking it to insulin signaling. Importantly, Tm7sf2 can control gene regulation in the liver, possibly through the protein’s ability to alter radial gene positioning within the nucleus (24). Moreover, Tm7sf2 controls the expression of several genes upstream and downstream in the cholesterol synthesis pathway (24). Because Tm7sf2 can affect both cholesterol biosynthesis and insulin sensitivity, we validated its upregulation by RT–quantitative PCR (qPCR) in a larger set of HFD-fed mouse livers (Fig. 5D).

Since Tm7sf2 was shown to alter Irs1/2 gene expression and positioning (24), we also tested for Irs1/2 mRNA expressions in mouse livers. Consistent with improved insulin signaling, we observed upregulated Irs2 mRNA expression in the HFD-fed TXNIP C247S mouse livers compared with WT and TXNIP KO mouse livers (Fig. 5E). On the other hand, we did not observe a significant difference in Irs1 mRNA expressions in the HFD-fed mouse livers (Fig. 5F). This finding agrees with prior studies that Irs2 plays a more dominant role in the liver and Irs1 in adipose tissue and skeletal muscles (37). Irs2 but not Irs1 is downregulated in the livers of subjects with metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (38) and obese subjects with type 2 diabetes (39). Notably, the upregulation of Tm7sf2 and Irs2 mRNA expressions in the livers of the TXNIP C247S mice was present only under HFD conditions but not under the control chow diet (Fig. 5, E–H). The increase in Tm7sf2 and Irs2 mRNA expressions in TXNIP C247S mouse livers also corresponded to a downregulation in Pck1 mRNA (Fig. 5I), which is the downstream target of the Irs2 pathway in the liver and suppresses gluconeogenesis (37, 39). We also detected higher Srebp2 mRNA expression in HFD-fed TXNIP C247S livers compared with WT and TXNIP KO mice, which is the upstream regulator of Tm7sf2 (Fig. S3P). These findings reveal Tm7sf2 as a potential mediator of improved hepatic insulin action in the HFD-fed TXNIP C247S mice.

After identifying Tm7sf2 as the potential mediator of insulin signaling in the livers of TXNIP C247S mice, specifically under HFD conditions, we sought to investigate whether Tm7sf2 controls insulin signaling in human liver cells under ROS stress. For this purpose, we used human HEPG2 cells that were transfected with either a Tm7sf2 plasmid or an empty vector control plasmid to overexpress the Tm7sf2 gene (Fig. S3R). We treated the oxidative stress group with 100 μM H2O2 to induce oxidative stress and stimulated the cells with human insulin. We chose to use H2O2 and not DTT since 100 μM H2O2 does not affect WT TXNIP–thioredoxin binding as DTT does (19). We observed the same outcomes as the mouse livers in the human liver cell line after ROS stress. Akt phosphorylation was increased only in redox-stress conditions (H2O2) by Tm7sf2 overexpression in HEPG2 cells compared with the empty vector group and not under the nonstressed condition (Fig. 6, A and B). Irs2 mRNA expression seemed to show a strong increasing expression trend (p = 0.054, ANOVA with post hoc multiple comparison testing) by Tm7sf2 overexpression with the oxidative stress in the H2O2-stimulated cells (Fig. 6C). Irs1 mRNA expression also appeared to be downregulated by Tm7sf2 overexpression with the oxidative stress in the H2O2-stimulated cells (Fig. 6D). The mRNA expressions of gluconeogenesis downstream target genes of Akt pathway in the liver, Pck1 and G6Pase, were also downregulated in the Tm7sf2-overexpressing cells but only under oxidative stress conditions (Fig. 6, E and F). Protein levels of PCK1–PEPCK were also lower in the Tm7sf2-overexpressing cells only under oxidative stress conditions (Fig. 6, G and H). Tm7sf2 can also control an anti-inflammatory response, and deletion of Tm7sf2 results in NF-κB activation and TNFα upregulation (25). Therefore, we also studied the NF-κB pathway in the HFD-fed mouse livers. We found that phosphorylation of both IkappaB kinase (IKK) and NF-κB p65 was decreased in TXNIP C247S mouse livers compared with WT controls and that downstream PKC activity was also decreased (Fig. S4, A–C). In addition, the Tnfa mRNA expression increase observed in HFD-fed WT mouse livers did not occur in TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO mice (Fig. S4D). We also observed a decrease in NLRP3 protein level in the livers of the TXNIP C247S group consuming the HFD, which did not occur in control groups (Fig. S4E).

Here, we also present clinical data of a family with some members carrying the heterozygous TXNIP C247S variant (Fig. 7A). The affected female patient was first evaluated in 2016 when she was 11 years old with a 2-year history of fever episodes accompanied by sore throat, abdominal pain, and headache. These symptoms largely disappeared over time. She presents normal body weight/body mass index value and normal plasma cholesterol and glucose levels. We obtained DNA from the patient and her parents for trio sequencing. The TXNIP C247S variant was inherited from her mother, who has a history of difficulty with weight loss and glucose intolerance. The mother presented abnormal weight, cholesterol, plasma glucose and blood pressure levels, which recovered following bariatric surgery. No other relative has been addressed regarding the C247S variant. The variant TXNIP (NM_006472.6):c.740G>C, p.(Cys247Ser), chr1:g.145994635C>G (hg38), is novel, with no previous documentation in population databases such as the 1000 Genomes Project, dbSNP, or the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD), version 4.1.0. Other variants of TXNIP C247 are observed in human databases. GnomAD, version 4.1.0 lists four other rare missense variants at the same codon: p.Cys247Trp (minor allele frequency [MAF]: 1.24e-6), p.Cys247Tyr (MAF: 6.20e-7), p.Cys247Gly (MAF: 1.24e-6), and p.Cys247Arg (MAF: 2.48e-6). Here, we show that the TXNIP–thioredoxin covalent interaction is necessary for developing HFD-induced hepatic insulin resistance. Among the altered cholesterol biosynthesis genes upregulated with the removal of the key C247 cysteine that allows the TXNIP–thioredoxin bond, the Tm7sf2 gene may play a key role in improving insulin signaling in mice and human liver cells (Fig. 7B). Furthermore, a heterozygous form of the TXNIP C247S variant appears well tolerated in humans. This suggests a specific evolutionarily conserved mechanism where redox state interacts with insulin resistance through this one specific cysteine in the TXNIP protein, presenting a key role. An HFD is known to induce ROS stress in organs, including the liver (40, 41), pancreas (42), intestines, and brain (43). While we did not observe a significant difference in glucose metabolism of TXNIP C247S mice compared with WT mice under a chow diet, the improved insulin sensitivity phenotype was clearly apparent after an HFD.

The TXNIP–thioredoxin interaction is important for diverse processes in mammals, including glucose metabolism and insulin signaling, inflammation, and mitochondrial metabolism (44). During the hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic assays, we assessed the insulin-stimulated glucose metabolism in liver, skeletal muscle, and white adipose tissues of the mice to define the major organ affected by the loss of TXNIP–thioredoxin interaction. According to results of hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic clamps, the liver was identified to be the main site that the increase in insulin sensitivity was mainly observed. We did not detect and increase in insulin sensitivity other major metabolic organs such as white adipose and skeletal muscle tissues.

The regulation of TXNIP activity is crucial for redox balance. However, TXNIP also regulates redox-independent physiological effects that directly influence pathophysiological processes, such as inflammatory responses, disrupted glucose metabolism, cellular senescence, and tumor development (21). Our laboratory has previously shown in vitro that TXNIP regulation of glucose uptake is independent of its interaction with thioredoxin. Also ARRDC4, a close homolog of TXNIP with a similar arrestin domain but does not interact with thioredoxin, also has the ability to inhibit glucose uptake (45). Therefore, it is possible that TXNIP might also regulate arrestin domain–dependent and redox-independent effects on glucose metabolism, potentially explaining the distinctive phenotypes observed in TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO mice. Thioredoxin interaction is critical for redox-dependent functions of TXNIP (21). The structure of the thioredoxin–TXNIP complex shows that the interaction occurs through a redox-dependent disulfide bond switching mechanism. TXNIP C63 and C247 residues are also critical for TXNIP dimer formation (20). Even though the interaction is abolished with TXNIP C247S mutation, we did not observe a difference in thioredoxin activity levels in the liver after an HFD in TXNIP C247S or TXNIP KO groups, consistent with previous studies (11). This result suggests that TXNIP is not serving as a thioredoxin inhibitor in this setting; instead, TXNIP may be sensing the redox state and changing its molecular binding partners, as suggested by mass spectrometry experiments (46, 47). However, it is possible that the C247S mutation alters lipid and glucose metabolism by making more unbound thioredoxin available, even though we did not detect a difference in thioredoxin activity.

We found elevated Irs2 expression but not Irs1 expression in the HFD-fed TXNIP C247S livers. This finding agreed with selective downregulation of IRS2 during insulin resistance in metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver diseases (38). IRS2 plays a more critical role in insulin signaling in the liver than IRS1, which dominates in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue (37), particularly in the suppression of gluconeogenesis genes (38). Significant downregulation of hepatic IRS2 but not IRS1 expression in obese individuals with type 2 diabetes was also observed in comparison with nondiabetic obese patients (39). Our data agree with these studies, since Irs2 expression was increased and gluconeogenic signaling was decreased in TXNIP C247S livers.

The limited number of genes with expressions altered significantly with TXNIP C247S mutation suggests that this single amino acid mutation explicitly regulates the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway genes, including Tm7sf2, which also acts as a liver-specific gene positioner (24). The TM7SF2/NET47 protein is a member of a protein family that includes more than a hundred transmembrane proteins that reside on the nuclear envelope and that are constantly trafficked between the endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear membranes (48). TM7SF2 is preferentially expressed in the liver (48) to control both the position and expression of liver metabolism–specific genes (24). Interestingly, in Tm7sf2-KO mice, which have insulin sensitivity, only a set of 26 genes changed position and expression (24), which agrees with our limited number of altered genes.

We found that Tm7sf2 mRNA expression was elevated in the livers of C247S mice specifically under an HFD. TM7SF2 itself can bind NADPH and act as an oxidoreductase (49). TM7SF2 is predicted to be a part of a receptor complex (Alliance of Genome Resources), and previous research has shown that it can interact with the redox sensor protein HSCARG/NmrA like redox sensor 1 (NMRAL1) that also binds NADP (26). TM7SF2’s elevation in livers and liver cell lines, specifically under ROS stress, and interaction with oxidative stress sensors, suggests that it could be serving as a part of a redox-sensing receptor complex that links intracellular redox state to insulin signaling.

Although our results suggested a role for Tm7sf2 in regulating insulin signaling during oxidative stress in liver cells, with a molecular response correlating with findings in the TXNIP C247S mice, in the light of the current data we cannot determine causality between the Tm7sf2 expression and the TXNIP C247S phenotype. To causally link the Tmsf72 gene to TXNIP C247S phenotype in mice further in vivo glucose metabolism experiments should be performed in double-transgenic Tm7sf2 KO/TXNIP C247S mice in future studies.

Even though cholesterol biosynthesis genes were upregulated, we did not observe a significant difference in plasma and liver cholesterol levels in TXNIP C247S mice. Liver cholesterol synthesis fuels the essential supply of animal cell plasma membranes and is very responsive to dietary cholesterol intake (∼100-fold), which in turn controls plasma cholesterol levels (50, 51). Therefore, it was unsurprising to find unaltered plasma cholesterol levels in these mice. Furthermore, a total KO of the Tm7sf2 gene in mice did not impair cholesterol biosynthesis (52) even though it controls both upstream and downstream cholesterol biosynthesis genes (52). The reason that Tm7sf2 KO mice did not have altered cholesterol levels was suggested to be due to LBR protein with redundant functions (22). Tm7sf2 and lamin-B receptor (lbr) genes emerged through a gene duplication event (53), and they share the same C14-sterol reductase activity (54). It was shown that Tm7sf2 expression levels showed an opposite trend compared with that of lbr in livers (54, 55). Expression of one could thus increase to compensate for the decrease of the other. This could contribute to the similar liver cholesterol levels in our mouse groups. Furthermore, in HFD-fed mouse livers, cholesterol synthesis genes were found to be downregulated, whereas plasma cholesterol levels were elevated (56), suggesting that expression of hepatic cholesterol synthesis genes does not reflect peripheral cholesterol profiles. Also in our model, the lipid changes observed in circulation did not seem to have a significant direct effect on insulin sensitivity.

The TXNIP C247S mutation was also found to significantly benefit visual acuity during retinitis pigmentosa in mice (57). The activation of the insulin pathway is beneficial to retinitis pigmentosa cone survival (58), so improving insulin signaling by TXNIP C247S mutation could contribute to this amelioration of sight. In addition, our TXNIP C247S mutation was global. Although we primarily observed glucose effects in the liver, an HFD would also alter cytokine and hormone profiles in adipose tissue. We cannot exclude interorgan crosstalk as a potential factor in these experiments.

The evolutionary basis for insulin resistance has been intensely debated for decades (59, 60, 61). One concept is evolutionary mismatch, where genetic changes that were initially advantageous in some manner, lead to insulin resistance in the modern setting of a calorie-dense diet (59, 62, 63). We speculate that mammals may have retained the TXNIP interaction with reduced thioredoxin through TXNIP C247, whereas amphibians, reptiles, and other animal classes lost this interaction. It is interesting that fish may have retained a different cysteine motif nearby; however, it is not known if the cysteine of TXNIP in fish allows covalent binding with thioredoxin. In settings of infection or injury, oxidative stress could promote hepatic insulin resistance to increase energy availability (62). Insulin resistance also progresses much faster during rapid growth periods such as puberty, possibly to enable energy redistribution (64, 65, 66). Thus, the TXNIP–thioredoxin interaction could potentially represent a mechanism for the redistribution of energy in times of stress, with possible detrimental cost of hepatic insulin resistance in the setting of a calorie-dense diet.

We generated a new TXNIP C247S mouse model using CRISPR–Cas9 technology. Our strategy was to swap the TGC codon in exon 5 of TXNIP that codes for the key cysteine to an AGT serine codon, and this change also creates an SpeI digestion site (Figs. 1B, S1A). Injections of the zygotes were carried out by the Genome Modification Facility at Harvard University. Zygotic pronuclei were microinjected with purified Cas9 mRNA (100 ng/μl), in vitro–transcribed synthetic guide RNAs (Synthego), and an asymmetrical ssDNA donor construct (IDT). Microinjected zygotes were implanted into C57BL/6J surrogate females. Genotypes were confirmed by restriction enzyme digestion and Sanger sequencing (Fig. S1, A and B), and 100% mutated mice were used as colony founders. Selected mice were bred with WT C57BL/6J mice, and pups were genotyped to confirm that the desired C247S mutation was incorporated into the germline. TLA sequencing was performed by Cergentis on cells from the frozen bone marrow of TXNIP C247S and WT controls that were processed according to Cergentis' TLA protocol (67) to check for off-target mutations. This analysis aimed to identify breakpoint sequences of the genomic modification(s) and assess the presence of structural variants surrounding the TXNIP locus. No other sequence and structural variants were detected in the TXNIP gene locus chr3:96,557,957-96,561,857 other than the desired mutation (Fig. S1C). Before experiments, mice were backcrossed in a C57BL/6J genetic background for several generations. WT siblings from the TXNIP C247S colony backcrosses were used to generate WT control mice. TXNIP KO mice were previously created by our laboratory (68). Male mice were used for metabolic studies involving insulin sensitivity because of increased variability in females because of hormonal changes (69). All mice were housed at a controlled temperature and a light–dark cycle with free access to a standard chow diet (Prolab IsoPro RMH 3000 5P75; LabDiet) or 60% HFD (D12492i; Research Diets) and water.

Mice were fasted for 16 h before GTTs and PTTs and 4 h before ITTs. Fasted mice were injected intraperitoneally with glucose (1 or 2 g/kg), pyruvate (1 or 2 g/kg), or insulin (0.75 or 1 IU/kg) according to their diet. Blood samples were collected via the tail vein, and glucose levels were measured using a handheld glucometer (Contour) at designated time points. Insulin stimulation was performed by injecting insulin (1 U/kg) i.p. and collecting liver tissues after 10 min.

HEPG2 human liver cell lines from American Type Culture Collection were cultured with a complete growth medium with Eagle’s minimum essential medium. Cells were transfected with EV or Tm7sf2 vector (NET47 pEGFP-N2 [593] was a gift from Eric Schirmer, Addgene plasmid #61986) using Lipofectamine 3000 reagent (Thermo Fisher). After 48 h, cells were starved in serum-free Eagle’s minimal essential medium for 4 h and were stimulated with 100 μM 30% H2O2 during the last 2 h. Later, cells were stimulated with 10 nm human insulin for 10 min and then collected, and protein and RNA samples were isolated.

Insulin levels were measured in 4-h fasted plasma using ELISA kits according to the manufacturer's protocol (Alpco; #NH80-INSMSU-E01). Liver thioredoxin activity was measured in liver lysates in a sample buffer using a modified protocol from Cayman Chemicals. Liver free fatty acids were measured in chow and 8-week HFD-fed mouse livers using a Free-fatty-acid Assay Kit (Abcam; #ab65341). PKC activity was measured by PKC Kinase Activity Assay Kit in liver lysates (Abcam; #ab139437). The kit measures the activity of all PKC isoforms. Liver triglycerides were measured in 8-week HFD-fed mouse livers using a Triglyceride assay kit (Abcam; #ab65336). Plasma and liver total and free cholesterol levels were measured using a Cholesterol quantification kit (Sigma–Aldrich; #MAK043). Plasma beta hydroxybutyrate levels were measured using ketone body kits (Abcam; #ab83390, #ab272541). Liver GSH/GSSG values were measured using GSH/GSSG Ratio Detection Kit II (Abcam; #ab205811).

Western blots were performed using Phospho-Akt (Ser473) (#9271), Akt (#9272), Beta-actin (#8457), Phospho-IKKa/b (#2697), IKKb (#8943), Phospho-NFkB p65 (#3033), NFkB p65 (#8242), Pck1 (#12940S), NLRP3 (#15101S), AMPKa (D5A2) (#5831) p-AMPKa (#2535), p-mTOR (#5536), and mTOR (#2972) antibodies (Cell Signaling). Protein bands were detected using an enhanced chemiluminescence substrate. Images were taken either using an automated processor (Bio-Rad) or with autoradiography films that were exposed in cassettes in a darkroom. Antibody validation was based on our previous publications, and preliminary experiments and expected molecular weights were observed. ImageJ (US National Institutes of Health [NIH], https://imagej.net/ij/, 1997–2018) software was used to quantify western blot images.

Lipidomic analysis of plasma samples was performed as described by Su et al. (70). Briefly, after the addition of an internal standard mix, lipids were extracted from plasma samples using an adjusted methyl tery-butyl ether–methanol extraction (71). Extracted lipids were concentrated and reconstituted in a mixture of dichloromethane:methanol (50:50) containing 10 mM ammonium acetate before shotgun lipidomic analysis. Samples were directly infused into the mass spectrometer using a Shimadzu HPLC (Nexera LC-30AD). Separation and targeted profiling of lipid species was performed by combining differential mobility spectrometry and a QTRAP system (QTRAP 5500; SCIEX) run in multiple reaction monitoring mode. Data analysis and absolute quantification of lipids were conducted using the Shotgun Lipidomics Assistant, a Python-based application that facilitates differential mobility spectrometry–based lipidomics workflow (70).

Mice that were fed 8 weeks of HFD were sacrificed, and liver tissues were collected. RNA was isolated using QIAGEN RNeasy Kits. RNA samples were processed by Azenta Biosciences for library preparation and Bulk RNASeq reads (Illumina). Bioinformatic analysis was performed using raw FASTQ as follows: The reads were trimmed for quality and adapters with Trimmomatic v0.39 (72) with the following parameters: LEADING:3 TRAILING:3 SLIDINGWINDOW:4:15 MINLEN:36. The standard Kallisto index was retrieved from Pachter Lab’s Github (https://github.com/pachterlab/kallisto-transcriptome-indices). Sequence-based bias correction was performed using Kallisto v0.50.1 (73) with 100 bootstraps. The transcript-level abundances from Kallisto were summarized and imported into R as a matrix of counts using tximport v1.0.3 (74). Differentially expressed genes were determined by estimating fold change and dispersion using DESeq2 (75). Pseudogenes and mitochondrial genes, as identified by Ensembl (76), were first removed from the dataset. Subsequently, the remaining data were filtered based on a p value threshold of 0.05, followed by a two-tailed t test with a significance level of 0.05. These significant genes were visualized using pheatmap, v1.0.12 (77) and ggplot2 v3.4.4 (78). Pathway analysis was performed using pathfindR (79) (v2.4.1) using the Kyoto Encylopedia of Genes and Genomes database (80). Reactome and WikiPathways enrichment analysis was performed using Enrichr, using The Reactome Pathways Knowledgebase 2024 and WikiPathways 2024 Mouse database, respectively. Bar charts of the results were plotted using Matplotlib and Seaborn using Enrichr Appyter.

For verification of RNA-Seq results, gene expressions were measured by RT–qPCR in a different cohort of mice. For RT–qPCR, RNA was extracted from homogenized liver samples and cells by the TRIzol (Life Sciences) method according to the manufacturer's protocol. The complementary DNA was synthesized from 2 μg of total RNA by use of the High-Capacity cDNA synthesis kit (Applied Biosystems), and reactions were performed using the Taqman gene expression assays (#Mm00840455, #Mm00443258, #Mm01277042, #Mm00514571, #Mm00501703, #Mm03038438, #Mm00440636, #Mm01233546, #Mm00839336, #Mm01278327, #Mm01337454, #Mm00477897, #Mm0490968, #Mm00436772, #Mm03012094, #Mm01306292, #Hs02802676, #Hs00159918, #Hs00427620, #Hs00178563, #Hs00275843, #Hs00162807, #Hs01098079; Thermo Fisher).

To generate the protein phylogeny tree in Figure 1, orthologs were pulled from Ortho DB v11 (81), National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) database, and UniProt (82). The sequences were compared with NCBI COBALT (83), and iTOL and phyloT (84) software were used for tree generation.

Hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic clamp experiments were conducted at the UMass Metabolic Disease Research Center using a primed and continuous infusion of human insulin (2.5 mU/kg/min), and glucose was infused at variable rates to maintain euglycemia (69). Briefly, whole-body glucose turnover was measured using a continuous infusion of [3-3H] glucose during the clamp, and HGP was determined by subtracting the glucose infusion rate from the whole-body glucose turnover. At the end of the clamps, mice were anesthetized and individual tissues were taken for biochemical analysis (69).

Data were expressed as means ± STD. The significance of the difference in mean values was determined using one-way and two-way ANOVA with Tukey and Bonferroni, Holm–Sidak post hoc tests, and Kruskal–Wallis test with Benjamini, Krieger, and Yekutieli corrections and Student's t test where applicable. The statistical significance was set at a p value of <0.05.
